Nature Microbiology.title: Inside the gut microbiome of manatees
Nature Microbiology.abstract: Nature Microbiology, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41564-026-02529-7An ultra-deep metagenomic atlas of the gut microbiome of manatees sheds light on the broad and previously unexplored microbial and viral diversity underlying aquatic herbivory. We identified specialized molecular strategies for aquatic plant biomass deconstruction and discovered a metabolic pathway that expands the current functional landscape of gut carbohydrate metabolism.

Water Research.title: Carbon availability and stability modulate chemoautotrophic carbon fixation in estuarine and coastal wetlands.
Water Research.abstract: Chemoautotrophic carbon fixation (CCF) is a critical pathway for microbial CO2 fixation; however, how carbon dynamics mediate the CCF process remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the influences of carbon availability, source, and stability on the CCF process in estuarine and coastal wetlands. CCF rates varied >20-fold, ranging from 7.6 to 177 ng C g-1 d-1 and decreasing with increasing organic carbon concentration. Autochthonous, marine, and terrestrial sources contributed 14.0-40.1%, 22.1-51.9%, and 22.1-60.0% of total organic carbon, respectively. Autochthonous carbon significantly correlated with iron-bound organic carbon (Fe-OC) concentration and CCF rate, suggesting that autochthonous carbon was crucial for Fe-OC formation and the chemoautotrophic process. The observed isotopic depletion of δ13C-SOC exhibited substantial consumption of labile organic carbon by anaerobic respiration, which was accompanied by the enhanced CCF rates. The isotopic enrichment of δ13C-Fe-OC and significant loss of Fe-OC indicated Fe-OC decoupling during anaerobic incubation. In addition, the relationship between CCF and carbon fraction was strongly influenced by the contrasting wetland habitats. Collectively, carbon availability and biogeochemical conditions jointly mediate chemoautotrophic activity, exerting a significant influence on allocation tradeoff and preferential preservation of organic carbon in estuarine and coastal wetlands.

Water Research.title: Enzyme-assisted bromination enables deep mineralization of trace urea by activating the rate-limiting intermediate.
Water Research.abstract: Bromination is practically applied for removing trace urea (μg·L-1) to meet the stringent requirements of electronic-grade ultrapure water, but it remains limited by slow kinetics at circumneutral pH, with the origin of this kinetic limitation not well understood. Here, the pH dependence of urea mineralization kinetics and pathways was systematically evaluated, while an enzyme-assisted bromination strategy was developed to relieve this limitation. The pH dependence was found to arise from bromination intermediates. Bromine reacts rapidly with urea regardless of pH, but the resulting monobromourea (pKa = 11.29) is brominated 55-fold more slowly in its neutral form than in its deprotonated form. Thus, it accumulates and dictates the overall rate below pH 10. Then, bromine was coupled with urea oligomerase to activate the accumulating intermediate rather than the parent compound. The enzyme did not alter the mineralization pathway or reaction order, but suppressed monobromourea accumulation and increased the apparent mineralization rate constant by 5.7-fold at pH 7.0. Theoretical calculations revealed that coordination of monobromourea at the dinickel site of enzyme polarizes its NH bond, conferring deprotonation-like electronic character and lowering the bromination barrier from 4.35 to 3.44 kcal·mol-1. Combined with downstream reverse osmosis, this approach can more efficiently polish the total organic carbon required for electronic-grade ultrapure water, demonstrating that targeting rate-limiting intermediates with enzyme-assisted bromination offers a general route to intensifying halogenation-based mineralization.

Water Research.title: Mechanisms of accelerated aging of microplastics and DOM release under cyclic environments: Underestimated environmental effects from freeze-thaw cycles.
Water Research.abstract: Microplastics (MPs) pollution is intensified by environmental aging. However, most studies have focused on individual aging conditions (e.g., continuous light or freezing), with less attention to the effects of cyclic environmental stressors on aging of MPs. Therefore, studying the impact of cyclic conditions on aging of MPs is of great significance for accurately reflecting their ecological risk. In this study, polystyrene (PS) and polylactic acid (PLA) were selected to systematically elucidate their aging mechanisms under light-dark alternation and freeze-thaw cycles, as well as the composition and characteristics of dissolved organic matter (DOM) released during aging. The results showed that, compared to their corresponding continuous conditions, light-dark alternation and freeze-thaw cycles increased the aging rate of MPs by 0.12-0.68-fold and 0.12-0.92-fold, respectively, suggesting that studies conducted under single aging conditions may underestimate their environmental impacts. Furthermore, compared with light-dark alternation, freeze-thaw cycles generated more reactive sites on MPs, thereby promoting hydrolysis and accelerating the aging of PLA-MPs (increased 0.46-fold). Distinct mechanisms were identified for the two cyclic aging processes: light-dark alternation primarily relies on light-driven •OH radicals, whereas freeze-thaw cycles are governed mainly by mechanical stress and/or hydrolysis. Meanwhile, freeze-thaw cycles generated less aromatic, higher-H/C DOM molecules, which have been reported to exhibit relatively high lability and potentially stronger short-term environmental disturbances. These findings highlight freeze-thaw cycles as an important driver of MP aging and associated DOM transformation, particularly for biodegradable plastics.

Water Research.title: Hydrology-guided intelligent spatiotemporal reconstruction method for sparse water quality data in urban watersheds.
Water Research.abstract: Nature-Based Systems are a critical approach to water management in urban watersheds. Assessing the effectiveness of such sustainable water management schemes depends fundamentally on sufficient and reliable water quality data. However, existing sparse monitoring networks lack continuous and reliable observation records, failing to meet the data requirements for monitoring spatiotemporal variations in water quality. Moreover, most conventional reconstruction methods are purely data-driven and lack the integration of hydrological knowledge, which hampers their capability to handle sparse observations in urban watersheds. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a deep learning-based spatiotemporal reconstruction framework for water-quality and hydrometeorological data. The framework first reconstructs missing hydrometeorological driving sequences. Subsequently, it leverages the reconstructed hydrological sequences to guide the reconstruction of water quality data, transforming sparse 4-hourly observations into complete hourly series. Finally, a probabilistic forecasting module is built upon the high-resolution reconstructed series, outputting Gaussian predictive means and standard deviations to quantify uncertainty and estimate the probability of exceeding water quality standards. The method is validated using field monitoring data from six stations in the Huaxi River watershed, Chongqing. Experimental results indicate that the reconstructed hourly water quality series outperform the original 4-hourly data in capturing pollutant concentration variability, with Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency improvements ranging from 0.18 to 0.57. These results demonstrate that the framework serves short-term probabilistic forecasting and early warning of water quality standard exceedances, providing timely data support for pollution risk management in urban watersheds. The code that supports the findings of this study is openly available in the HG-STGNN repository on GitHub at https://github.com/Indig0Cat/HG-STGNN.

Water Research.title: Membrane distillation for sustainable freshwater-heat co-generation from geothermal brine in cold regions.
Water Research.abstract: As cold regions face growing demands for freshwater and space heating, geothermal brines offer a unique dual-resource advantage by supplying both thermal energy and viable desalination feedwater. However, the existing exploitation of this resource relies primarily on separate heat exchangers and thermal desalination processes, which are limited by singular functionality, low efficiency and scaling susceptibility. To fully harness this renewable energy potential, we develop a geothermal-driven multistage air-gap membrane distillation (AGMD) system for simultaneous freshwater production and heat extraction. During the process, the geothermal brine undergoes phase changes (i.e., evaporation-condensation) to yield freshwater, while the vapor-released latent heat is recovered, thereby achieving the freshwater-heat co-generation. The feasibility is demonstrated through coupled experiments and simulations, and by balancing the trade-off between system performance and capital cost, we identify a 16-stage configuration as the optimal design. Validated real-world simulations across 15 northern provinces in China confirm the high operational stability and broad deployability of the proposed system. Economically, for community-scale heating (100000 kWh day-1), the cogeneration cost is reduced to $0.0036 kWh-1, which is generally more than 20% below local market heating prices. Ultimately, our work provides a practical pathway for integrating geothermal utilization, freshwater supply and space heating in community services.

Water Research.title: Triplet-state dissolved organic matter drives solar reduction photochemistry through sulfite activation.
Water Research.abstract: Sulfite (S(IV)) activation has emerged as a promising strategy for micropollutant abatement, yet whether naturally occurring dissolved organic matter (DOM) can efficiently activate S(IV) and which reactive species are responsible for micropollutant transformation remain unclear. Here, using imidacloprid (IMI) as a model micropollutant, we demonstrate a pronounced synergistic effect between DOM photosensitization and S(IV) activation, increasing the observed IMI degradation rate constant to 5.21 times that in the Solar-S(IV) process. Triplet-state DOM (3DOM*) was identified as the primary species responsible for S(IV) activation. Laser flash photolysis tests with model photosensitizers revealed fast reactions between triplet species and S(IV), with second-order quenching rate constants ranging from 4.80(± 0.30) × 107 M-1 s-1 to 1.85(± 0.40) × 109 M-1 s-1 at pH 7.0. S(IV) activation by 3DOM* proceeds predominantly through electron transfer, while proton-coupled electron transfer provides an additional pathway that accelerates bisulfite activation. The long-overlooked sulfite radical (SO3•-), rather than conventional oxidizing radicals, was identified as the dominant species governing IMI degradation via reduction and radical-addition reactions. Collectively, these findings redefine 3DOM* as a photoredox mediator initiating reductive sulfur photochemistry, thereby establishing a mechanistic foundation for sustainable, solar-driven advanced reduction processes applicable to both natural and engineered aquatic environments.

Water Research.title: Membrane-aerated biofilm reactors (MABRs) are enriched with filamentous fungi at high carbon concentrations.
Water Research.abstract: Membrane-aerated biofilm reactors (MABRs) are an energy-efficient wastewater treatment technology based on biofilms grown on gas-permeable membranes. As with most wastewater treatment technologies, MABR biofilms are typically dominated by bacteria. However, here we show that MABRs supplied with high organic carbon loadings can be dominated by filamentous fungi, leading to stiff biofilms. When fed with food processing wastewater at approximately 550 mg COD L⁻¹, filamentous fungi accounted for 85% of the biofilm, compared to 30% for co-diffusional controls. The MABR biofilms showed EPS matrices enriched in protein and extracellular DNA, and were stiffer than co-diffusional biofilms. When supplied with 550 mg COD L⁻¹ acetate in minimal medium, filamentous fungi accounted for 67% of the biofilm and were dominated by Geotrichum and Galactomyces. In contrast, MABRs supplied with 150 mg COD L⁻¹ acetate had only 4% filamentous fungi. These findings identify filamentous fungi as important and overlooked members of MABR biofilms, especially for high carbon loadings. A potential benefit is that fungi can degrade recalcitrant compounds not degraded by bacteria. However, the biofilm's greater mechanical strength may lead to excessive biofilm accumulation and may require special measures to promote detachment.

Water Research.title: Surfactants as dynamic regulators of contaminant transport: From interfacial processes to groundwater remediation outcomes.
Water Research.abstract: Surfactants enter subsurface environments through remediation, industrial releases, wastewater infiltration, biological production, and consumer products. Their effects on contaminant fate are commonly interpreted through micellar solubilization and reduction of fluid-fluid interfacial tension. Whether these processes improve recovery or increase spreading depends on contaminant-bearing phase mobility, hydraulic contact and capture. By partitioning among aqueous, solid, fluid-fluid, and particle-associated domains, surfactants alter wettability, capillary forces, surface charge, sorption, colloidal stability, and carrier mobility, thereby redistributing contaminant mass among transport states with different mobilities. Here we synthesize these processes across molecular, pore, column, and aquifer scales and propose a conceptual diagnostic framework termed Surfactant-Interface-Mobility (SIM). SIM links the local formulation state, dynamic interfacial response and area, contaminant-state redistribution, phase-specific mobility, and hydraulic accessibility. Four diagnostic transport categories-retention, aqueous transfer including solubilization, nonaqueous-phase liquid (NAPL) mobilization, and carrier-facilitated transport-can coexist and evolve. Under effective hydraulic capture, surfactant-induced transitions can increase contaminant recovery; inadequate contact can leave source mass untreated, while inadequate capture can allow redistribution, plume expansion or downstream exposure. SIM organizes the measurements needed to distinguish these outcomes. Its predictive capability and incremental value relative to established transport models require independent validation.

Water Research.title: A quaternary ammonium-modified colloidal activated carbon for effective and selective capture of PFOA in groundwater: Mechanisms of multi-synergistic adsorption interactions.
Water Research.abstract: Based on the unique properties of perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), we developed a carbon-based adsorbent strategy by tailoring pore structures and introducing synergistic electrostatic, hydrophobic, and Lewis acid sites, leading to the fabrication of quaternary ammonium-modified colloidal activated carbon (QA-CAC) for PFOA adsorption in groundwater. QA-CAC exhibited superior PFOA adsorption capacity compared to commercial CAC, achieving over 90% removal within 3 min. According to Freundlich isotherm fitting, the adsorption capacity (Kf) reached 102.62 (mg/g)(mg/L)-0.49. When competing pollutants of various types coexisted, QA-CAC exhibited selective adsorption toward PFOA. Density functional theory calculations demonstrated that PFOA possessed a distinct thermodynamic preference over competing contaminants, with the strongest adsorption affinity and an adsorption energy of -2.93 eV. Common groundwater constituents did not significantly interfere with the adsorption capacity for PFOA. An artificial groundwater system was also selected to evaluate the adsorption and desorption performance of QA-CAC toward PFOA. Under different water matrices and external contaminants, PFOA previously adsorbed onto QA-CAC exhibited an extremely low desorption risk. Furthermore, QA-CAC suspension maintained excellent stability even after 20 days, and exhibited significantly enhanced mobility in simulated column. This work provides guidance for the design of efficient carbon-based adsorbents for in situ remediation of PFOA-contaminated groundwater.

Nature Genetics.title: Multiancestry genome-wide association and integrative multiomics analyses implicate key pathways in endometriosis
Nature Genetics.abstract: Nature Genetics, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41588-026-02810-9Multiancestry genome-wide association coupled with integrative multiomics analyses identify risk loci for endometriosis and implicate key genes and pathways underlying its pathogenesis, including roles for immune cell types and cellular proliferation.

Nature Water.title: Beyond selectivity in ion separations
Nature Water.abstract: Nature Water, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s44221-026-00755-1Selectivity is the dominant metric for ion-selective separations, yet it often fails to predict process performance by itself. A new framework allows for a more reliable comparison between processes based on multiple separation outcomes.

eLife.title: Ramping-up hippocampal ripples and their neocortical coupling support human visual short-term memory
eLife.abstract: Emerging evidence suggests that the hippocampus contributes to visual short-term memory (VSTM). However, the neural mechanisms through which hippocampal activity supports the maintenance of VSTM representations remain largely unknown. Here, using intracranial EEG recordings from human participants performing a delayed match-to-sample task for naturalistic objects, we investigated the role of hippocampal ripple activity—brief high-frequency oscillations associated with memory replay—in VSTM maintenance and hippocampal-neocortical communication. We found that hippocampal ripple rates progressively ramped up during the maintenance period and supported successful VSTM. More critically, hippocampal ripples were temporally coupled with the ripples in the lateral temporal lobe (LTL), and these coupled ripples were associated with memory reactivation in the LTL. These findings provide direct evidence that hippocampal–neocortical interaction via coupled ripples supports VSTM, extending the role of hippocampal ripples from long-term consolidation to short-term mnemonic processes and offering new insights into the dynamic coding mechanisms of working memory.

Nature Reviews Microbiology.title: A voyage of viral transmission
Nature Reviews Microbiology.abstract: Nature Reviews Microbiology, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41579-026-01399-4This study provides further evidence of Andes virus human-to-human transmission, specifically in close-contact settings.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: SynCED: the Synthetic Chemical Exposome Database.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The Synthetic Chemical Exposome Database (SynCED) (https://syncedb.ca) is a substantially updated and expanded version of the Toxin and Toxin Target Database (T3DB). SynCED provides rich data on 316 418 synthetic chemicals from diverse chemical, toxicological, exposure, and regulatory sources. The synthetic chemical exposome comprises a vast and rapidly expanding range of anthropogenic chemicals, yet information on their sources, uses, biological effects, toxicity, and molecular interactions remains fragmented across numerous resources. SynCED addresses this problem by consolidating this information and linking most known synthetic chemicals with standardized chemical names and identifiers, compound descriptions, predicted or measured physicochemical properties, reference spectral data, exposure and use information, toxicological data, and biological targets or interactions. Literature-derived compound descriptions and functional annotations were built using the Chemical Functional Ontology (ChemFOnt) Fact Finder pipeline, which extracts semantically defined chemical-relation-entity associations while retaining supporting evidence and provenance. In addition to literature-derived biological target information, SynCED also incorporates ligand-based protein-target predictions to extend the coverage of chemicals lacking experimentally characterized interactions. To facilitate compound identification using non-target or suspect screening, SynCED provides extensive search utilities supporting searches by chemical structure, toxicity, text, mass, molecular weight, elemental composition, ESI-MS, EI-MS, and NMR spectra (both measured and predicted) as well as searches by target sequence (protein and DNA). It also supports database browsing by chemical names, ClassyFire chemical taxonomy and exposure source. Together, these features extend T3DB to turn SynCED into a broader, more provenance-aware database, that supports suspect or non-target screening, chemical exposure and hazard assessment, mechanistic studies, and general chemical exposomics research.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: FusionGDB 3.0: integrating breakpoints, generating personalized sequences, and inferring tumorigenic scenarios for human fusion genes.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: FusionGDB has served diverse biological, health, and clinical research communities as a unique functional annotation knowledgebase of human fusion genes. In this study, we report an updated resource of human fusion gene annotation (FusionGDB 3.0), available at https://compbio.uth.edu/FusionGDB/. FusionGDB 3.0 includes substantial content updates: 156K up-to-date human fusion genes established by integrating 216K RNA-seq-based and 100K WGS-based breakpoint events, comprehensive open reading frame annotations, protein domain retention searches, and 1.13 million personalized fusion protein sequences reflecting individual nsSNVs from TCGA and CCLE, as well as N- and C-truncated protein sequences alongside canonical in-frame products. Furthermore, it incorporates 18K potential tumorigenic scenarios, supported by evidence from the literature, spanning drug-targetable gene group fusions, the epigenomic architecture around breakpoint junctions, and therapeutic prioritization scoring. FusionGDB 3.0 establishes a systematic framework for the functional annotation of coding structural variants. FusionGDB 3.0 serves as a pivotal reference knowledgebase for the genomics, oncology, and precision pharmacology communities, while also functioning as a foundational benchmark dataset for training and validating machine learning models, structural biology platforms, and AI-driven therapeutic discovery pipelines.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: CIViC 2026: expanding cancer variant curation with AI, genome-wide biomarkers, and genomic regions.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The CIViC (Clinical Interpretations of Variants in Cancer) knowledgebase (https://civicdb.org) remains one of the few free, unrestricted knowledgebases for the distribution of somatic cancer variant interpretations. CIViC leverages public curation and expert moderation to address the bottleneck problem of cancer variant interpretation for patient care. As the curation platform for ClinGen Somatic Cancer, the CIViC knowledge model is informed by multiple experts across disparate fields in cancer and, in turn, acts as a model for cancer variant classification and representation. In order to capture a wider range of genomic variations, several updates to CIViC's data and curation model have been made with a focus on maintaining familiar workflows and user interface layouts. A new top-level entity called the Feature represents Genes, Fusions, Regions for large-scale structural variations, and Factors for genome-wide biomarkers. Accompanying Variants capture information unique to each genomic event. Molecular Profiles enable the curation of complex combinations of these Variants. CIViC has also developed a system for approval and submission of Assertions to ClinVar, guidance for the use of AI in curation and moderation of content, and additional capabilities such as source retraction monitoring and an advanced query builder.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: CovPDB 2.0: an expanded covalent protein-ligand interactome.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The rational design of covalently binding inhibitors to specifically block selected target proteins has become a common strategy in drug discovery. Such design is based on structural insights into how electrophilic ligands bind to nucleophilic residues. CovPDB v1.0 provided high-resolution cocrystal structures of biologically relevant covalent protein-ligand complexes curated from the Protein Data Bank. Here, we describe CovPDB v2.0, a substantially extended release that addresses three main limitations of the original resource. First, to reflect the numerous novel covalently binding ligands developed and structurally elucidated over the past 4 years, we have classified, annotated, and integrated these entries into the database. This expands the collection from ~2300 to ~6200 protein-ligand complexes, comprising ~3600 pre-reactive ligands, ~1300 target proteins, 119 warheads, and 27 reaction types. Second, we expanded the structural scope beyond experimental cocrystals by generating AlphaFold3 cofolding models for additional ~6800 covalent complexes for which we had experimental evidence for a covalent ligand binding. Third, we added ~7100 non-covalent complexes in which the binding-site cysteines are annotated with a predicted reactivity and ligandability scores. A redesigned web interface allows users to browse, filter, and cross-search experimental, modelled, and ligandable-cysteine entries. CovPDB 2.0 is freely accessible at https://www.pharmbioinf.uni-freiburg.de/covpdb.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: canSAR 2026-an update to the public drug discovery knowledgebase.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: canSAR (https://cansar.ai) serves as the world's largest public platform for cancer drug discovery and translational research. It serves as an exploration and hypothesis generation platform for drug discovery through (i) fully integrating large, multidisciplinary data from public resources, as well as bespoke curated data, creating a connected, navigable drug discovery knowledge map; and (ii) applying a suite of machine learning and AI tools to generate novel insights. We share the latest updates to canSAR highlighting growth across all data, enhancements to the predictive algorithms, and continued improvements to the user experience. We leverage our latest open science chemical handling and druggability prediction tools to provide traceable insights. An increased focus of the platform is to provide "in-line" support and guidance to drug discovery exploration. We report the first incarnation of our high-fidelity, agentic-AI-generated, context-specific summaries, which we provide across the website for all human proteins to further aid users in synthesis and distillation of key information.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Europe PMC in 2026.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Europe PMC (https://europepmc.org/) is an open access database of life-science literature that delivers open science to a wide audience through an open web interface, APIs, and bulk downloads. It brings together 48 million abstracts, 12 million full text published articles, and supplementary files and 1.2 million preprints, 76 000 of them full text, and makes them findable through dozens of search axes. Europe PMC is supported by 35 European and international funders to deliver a global open infrastructure and support their open access policies and metrics analysis. Europe PMC enriches the literature with 2 billion text-mined annotations, and links to dozens of biological databases. New developments to the Europe PMC platform since the last database update in 2023 include: (i) harnessing AI to enhance discovery through new machine learning generated annotations and working towards Europe PMC as a knowledge layer for LLMs; (ii) enhancing product development UX/UI capabilities, showcased through a new advanced search; (iii) improving literature discovery by text mining supplementary files; (iv) improving persistent identifier coverage and expanding the citation network.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: DriverDBv5: a multi-omics integration database for cancer driver gene research.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Cancer is driven by alterations across multiple molecular layers, but whether multi-omics drivers carry prognostic weight has received little systematic attention. DriverDBv5 (https://driverdb.bioinfomics.org/) extends DriverDB from driver identification to prognostic evaluation. It has been expanded to 187 cohorts, 43 862 patients, and 129 655 samples, with 154 cohorts from non-TCGA (The Cancer Genome Atlas) repositories reconciled by a generalized multi-omics barcode. Driver genes can be evaluated with Cox and mixture cure models, with machine learning on the full multi-omics feature matrix, and for the joint prognostic effect of alterations in two omics layers. The Customized Analysis module has grown from 4 to 10 tools for user-defined gene sets, subgroups, and covariates, and a human body map offers an anatomical entry point. DriverDBv5 thus reveals not only which alterations drive a tumor, but also which of them relate to patient outcome.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: ADCdb 2.0: clinical landscape and ADMET profiles of antibody-drug conjugates.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Systematically characterizing antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) is essential for understanding their therapeutic properties, guiding molecular design, and supporting clinical development. Recently, the expanding clinical landscape of ADCs has generated extensive information on target antigens, therapeutic indications, and clinical trial pipelines, providing a valuable foundation for informing ADC development strategies. Moreover, ADMET profiles are critical for understanding the in vivo disposition, efficacy, and safety of ADCs. Integrating these accumulating clinical and pharmacological data is therefore necessary to enrich the evidence available for ADC development. In this study, ADCdb was updated to provide (i) detailed clinical landscape information for 542 ADCs, together with >3000 manually curated clinical trials from registries across nine registries and clinical trial platforms; (ii) >4000 ADMET profiles, including quantitative pharmacokinetic parameters and descriptive annotations supported by relevant references; and (iii) expanded pharmacological information and biological activity data comprising 13 088 ADC entries and 24 821 activity records, as well as ADC-specific functional annotations for 389 ADCs. Interactive visualization tools and antigen- and disease-centered search modules further enable systematic exploration of ADC composition, therapeutic indications, and clinical development. ADCdb 2.0 is expected to serve as a valuable resource for rational optimization of ADCs, and is accessible at https://idrblab.org/adcdb/.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: LACA: a cross-species single-cell resource for exploring longevity and aging-associated cellular and molecular programs.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Different species can have various maximum lifespans, some with exceptional longevity, yet the underlying cellular and molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Despite rapid advances in single-cell transcriptomics, resources that systematically connect single-cell gene expression profiles to species lifespan are limited. We hereby present the Longevity & Aging Cell Atlas (LACA), a database that integrates single-cell transcriptomic datasets across 134 species with their maximum lifespans. LACA includes over 148 million cells with 190 annotated cell types from single-cell datasets. LACA also has a cross-species analytical toolbox of longevity gene comparison, gene-lifespan correlation, and cell-lifespan correlation. These tools allow researchers to better interpret both evolutionarily conserved longevity mechanisms and the evolution of species-specific adaptations in longevity mechanisms without extensive computational expertise. LACA also provides a centenarian single-cell atlas and a human immune aging multi-omics atlas, demonstrating the analytical capability of the resource, as well as 11 different modules for longevity-related analysis, an integrated knowledge graph including curated longevity knowledge bases, and a retrieval-augmented research agent to further facilitate functional interpretation. The database is freely available at https://www.longevityaging.net/ or http://8.142.154.29/LACA/.

Nature Astronomy.title: The nature of the Norma arm as a bar-driven star-forming shock front
Nature Astronomy.abstract: Nature Astronomy, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41550-026-03010-5The Norma spiral arm reveals that stars can form under very diverse conditions in the Universe. Galaxy simulations suggest that masers, historically attributed to the Norma arm and more recently associated with bar orbits, may actually trace the Galactic bar shock front.

Nature Ecology & Evolution.title: Meta-analysis shows that immunization reduces amphibian susceptibility to the chytrid fungus
Nature Ecology & Evolution.abstract: Nature Ecology & Evolution, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41559-026-03221-zMeta-analysis of findings across 22 amphibian species shows efficacious experimental immunization with live Bd pathogens, and identifies differing effects on infection dynamics depending on immunization approach, host life stages and taxonomy.

Nature Communications.title: Optical observation of ultrafast carrier separation in InGaN photocatalyst nanostructures
Nature Communications.abstract: Nature Communications, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79779-wThe authors show that ultrafast carrier separation causes the rapid photoluminescence decay in nanostructured InGaN photocatalysts from time resolved photoluminescence and differential reflectance spectroscopy supported by numerical modelling.

Nature Communications.title: SMC5/6 safeguards chromatin compartments and TAD boundaries for genome stability
Nature Communications.abstract: Nature Communications, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79493-7The SMC5/6 complex protects genome stability, but how it shapes 3D genome folding is unclear. Here, the authors show that SMC5/6 loss in human cells alters chromatin compartments and activates inflammatory and cancer-related genes, changes that are uncoupled from DNA damage.

Nature Communications.title: Double-membrane-spanning RNA export pores are a conserved feature in nidovirus replication organelles
Nature Communications.abstract: Nature Communications, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78986-9This study shows that arteriviruses, like coronaviruses, form pore complexes that span their double-membrane replication organelles, pointing to a conserved nidovirus strategy that links the synthesis, export and packaging of viral RNA.

Nature Communications.title: σ-complex stabilization shapes enzymatic C-glycosylation and restricts the scope of natural C-glycosides
Nature Communications.abstract: Nature Communications, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79637-9Enzymes offer a sustainable route to C-glycosides, valuable compounds containing hydrolytically stable C-C bonds, but few are known to display C-glycosylation activity and their mechanism remains unclear. Here, the authors investigate a C-glycosyltransferase from maize, ZmUGT708A6, reveal two flexible gates that control substrate access and reactive conformations, and suggest that substrate hydroxylation patterns, protonation states, and σ-complex energetics restrict the scope of C-glycosides.

Nature Communications.title: High-κ bismuth molybdate single-crystalline dielectric for high-temperature two-dimensional transistors
Nature Communications.abstract: Nature Communications, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79576-5High temperature stability is an important requirement for future electronic circuits based on 2D semiconductors. Here, the authors report the synthesis of high-κ (54.2) Bi2MoO6 single-crystalline nanosheets and their application as gate dielectric for 2D MoS2 transistors, showing good thermal stability of the devices up to 500 K.

Nature Communications.title: var2csa transcription implicates variant surface antigen switching in cerebral malaria pathogenesis
Nature Communications.abstract: Nature Communications, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78682-8In this study, the authors report case-control studies in Mali and Malawi showing that cerebral malaria is associated with increased transcription of var2csa and EPCR-ICAM1 dual binding PfEMP1s, rather than EPCR-binding variants alone suggesting that var gene regulation may be a driver of severe disease.

Nature Communications.title: Pathway-dependent chiral toroid self-assembly and topological transformations based on large π-conjugated dipeptides
Nature Communications.abstract: Nature Communications, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79527-0Rational introduction of large π-conjugated moieties to peptides is crucial for their assembly, luminescence, chiral expression, and functional applications. Here the authors functionalize a series of dipeptides with large conjugated benzoperylene imide segments demonstrating programmable chiroptical and self-assembly behaviors.

Nature Communications.title: Intravenous phage therapy for difficult-to-treat infections: a systematic review and meta-analysis of individual patient data

Biogeosciences.title: Building a random forest machine learning model for annual Net Ecosystem Exchange estimation in agricultural fields using discontinuous atmospheric Eddy Covariance measurements
Biogeosciences.abstract: Building a random forest machine learning model for annual Net Ecosystem Exchange estimation in agricultural fields using discontinuous atmospheric Eddy Covariance measurements Camille Pery, Pierre Polsenaere, Eric Lamaud, Natacha Volto, Nathalie Long, Jonathan Deborde, Shunko Bolsée, Olivier Philippine, Vona Méléder, and Christine Dupuy Biogeosciences, 23, 8477–8505, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8477-2026, 2026 This study evaluates the potential of combining continuous atmospheric CO2 flux measurements with IA modelling to estimate carbon budgets in agricultural crops in a French wetland. Modelling strategies were developed to capture their phenological and management-related carbon dynamics. Our results provide a pragmatic framework to derive plot-scale carbon budgets and offers promising perspectives for improving regional carbon flux inventories and assessing climate-smart agricultural practices.

Biogeosciences.title: Evaluating GNSS-T VOD sensitivity to plant water dynamics, rainfall interception, and dew in a coniferous forest
Biogeosciences.abstract: Evaluating GNSS-T VOD sensitivity to plant water dynamics, rainfall interception, and dew in a coniferous forest Konstantin Schellenberg, Sinikka J. Paulus, Ronald Queck, David Chaparro, Oliver Binks, Maurizio Mencuccini, Sharath S. Paligi, Henrik Hartmann, Christiane Schmullius, Clémence Dubois, and Thomas Jagdhuber Biogeosciences, 23, 8507–8536, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8507-2026, 2026 We evaluated Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals to monitor forest water storage, helping to close an important observational gap in plant hydraulics and micrometeorology at stand-scale. We show that signal losses in the canopy are strongly linked to three-dimensionally modeled rainfall interception. However, detecting subtle fluxes, such as internal water dynamics, dew and intercepted light rain is inhibited by signal noise, and the hydraulics properties of the ecosystem.

Biogeosciences.title: Climate warming-induced agricultural nitrous oxide emissions can offset mitigation benefits of fertiliser reduction
Biogeosciences.abstract: Climate warming-induced agricultural nitrous oxide emissions can offset mitigation benefits of fertiliser reduction Jize Jiang, Lenny H. E. Winkel, Andrea Stenke, Magdalena Necpalova, Moritz Laub, Iris Feigenwinter, Nina Buchmann, and Johan Six Biogeosciences, 23, 8537–8557, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8537-2026, 2026 We studied how fertiliser management and a warming climate affect nitrous oxide emissions from agricultural soils in Switzerland over the past fourty years. Using computer simulations and nationwide data, we found that lower fertiliser use reduced emissions, but rising temperatures cancelled part of these mitigations. The results show a trade-off between mitigation actions and environmental-driven feedback, highlighting future efforts must also account for the effects of a changing climate.

Science Bulletin.title: Non-Bloch exceptional points detached from branch points.
Science Bulletin.abstract: Exceptional points (EPs) in non-Hermitian Bloch band structures are branch points of the energy Riemann surface, connected pairwise by non-Hermitian Fermi arcs whose topology determines eigenvalue knots. Under open boundary conditions (OBCs), non-Hermitian skin effects enforce complex momenta and yield non-Bloch band structures, where EPs absent from the periodic spectrum-termed non-Bloch EPs-can emerge. Here, we show theoretically and experimentally that non-Bloch EPs are detached from branch points and instead emerge at saddle points of generalized-Brillouin-zone (GBZ) geometry within a single Riemann sheet. By identifying each band's sub-GBZ as a band-dependent base manifold, the parameter space over which its energy is defined, we establish general criteria for the emergence of such non-Bloch EPs in multiband systems. Using a reciprocal non-Hermitian Lieb lattice with geometry-dependent skin effects, we demonstrate that a change from rectangular to parallelogram geometry induces such non-Bloch EPs at energies distinct from any Bloch EP. In non-Bloch band structures, branch points carrying OBC eigenenergies do not produce EPs but instead appear as Whitney cusps-geometric singularities that anchor non-Bloch Fermi arcs and continue to govern eigenvalue knots. Measurements of these knots confirm the detachment of non-Bloch EPs from branch points, in sharp contrast to Bloch systems where the two are unified. Our results decouple non-Bloch EPs from the braiding topology associated with Fermi arcs and reveal the fundamental role of band-dependent base manifolds in reshaping non-Hermitian band structures.
